established.name: Mastadenovirus blackbeardi
established.headline: Human adenovirus B types including HAdV-3, -7, -11. Pneumonia, pharyngoconjunctival fever, haemorrhagic cystitis.

established.name: Mastadenovirus caesari
established.headline: Human adenovirus A/C types including HAdV-1, -2, -5. Respiratory illness and, in the immunocompromised, disseminated disease.

established.name: Mastadenovirus dominans
established.headline: Human adenovirus D types including HAdV-8, -19, -37. Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.

established.name: Mastadenovirus exoticum
established.headline: Human adenovirus E, HAdV-4. Acute respiratory disease, notably in military recruits.

established.name: Mastadenovirus faecale
established.headline: Human adenovirus F, HAdV-40 and -41. Infantile gastroenteritis.

established.name: Mastadenovirus russelli
established.headline: Human adenovirus G, HAdV-52. Gastroenteritis.

established.name: Mammarenavirus choriomeningitidis
established.headline: Globally distributed arenavirus of house mice; a neglected cause of aseptic meningitis and of severe congenital infection.

established.name: Mammarenavirus juninense
established.serogroup: New World clade B (haemorrhagic fever group)
established.headline: Cause of Argentine haemorrhagic fever; notable for an effective live-attenuated vaccine and proven immune plasma therapy.

established.name: Mammarenavirus lassaense
established.headline: Rodent-borne arenavirus causing 100,000–300,000 infections and thousands of deaths annually in West Africa.

established.name: Mammarenavirus brazilense
established.serogroup: New World clade B (haemorrhagic fever group)
established.headline: Sabiá virus. Brazilian haemorrhagic fever; laboratory infections recorded.

established.name: Mammarenavirus chapareense
established.serogroup: New World clade B (haemorrhagic fever group)
established.headline: Chapare virus. Bolivian haemorrhagic fever with nosocomial transmission.

established.name: Mammarenavirus guanaritoense
established.serogroup: New World clade B (haemorrhagic fever group)
established.headline: Guanarito virus. Venezuelan haemorrhagic fever.

established.name: Mammarenavirus lujoense
established.headline: Lujo virus. Nosocomial haemorrhagic fever outbreak in southern Africa.

established.name: Mammarenavirus machupoense
established.serogroup: New World clade B (haemorrhagic fever group)
established.headline: Machupo virus. Bolivian haemorrhagic fever.

established.name: Mamastrovirus hominis
established.headline: Human astrovirus 1-8. Paediatric gastroenteritis.

established.name: Norovirus norwalkense
established.headline: Norwalk virus. The dominant cause of epidemic non-bacterial gastroenteritis worldwide.

established.name: Sapovirus sapporoense
established.headline: Sapporo virus. Acute gastroenteritis in children and in outbreak settings.

established.name: Betacoronavirus pandemicum
established.headline: Sarbecovirus subgenus; SARS-CoV caused the 2002–2004 SARS epidemic and SARS-CoV-2 the COVID-19 pandemic.

established.name: Alphacoronavirus amsterdamense
established.headline: Human coronavirus NL63. Common cold and croup in young children.

established.name: Alphacoronavirus chicagoense
established.headline: Human coronavirus 229E. Common cold.

established.name: Betacoronavirus cameli
established.headline: MERS-CoV. Severe respiratory disease acquired from dromedary camels.

established.name: Betacoronavirus gravedinis
established.headline: Human coronavirus OC43. Common cold; occasional severe lower respiratory disease.

established.name: Betacoronavirus hongkongense
established.headline: Human coronavirus HKU1. Common cold and bronchiolitis.

established.name: Orthoebolavirus zairense
established.headline: Filovirus causing Ebola disease, with case fatality historically 25–90%; now treatable with monoclonal antibodies and preventable by vaccination.

established.name: Orthomarburgvirus marburgense
established.headline: The first filovirus recognised (Marburg, 1967), with case fatality in outbreaks of 24–88%; no licensed vaccine or therapeutic.

established.name: Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense
established.headline: Bundibugyo virus. Ebola disease outbreaks in Uganda and DRC.

established.name: Orthoebolavirus sudanense
established.headline: Sudan virus. Ebola disease outbreaks in East Africa.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus denguei
established.headline: The most important arboviral infection of humans worldwide, with an estimated 100–400 million infections annually.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus flavi
established.headline: The prototype flavivirus and the reason the genus is named 'flavi' — a vaccine-preventable viral haemorrhagic fever.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus japonicum
established.headline: The leading cause of vaccine-preventable viral encephalitis in Asia.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus kyasanurense
established.headline: Tick-borne flavivirus causing haemorrhagic fever in the Western Ghats of India, with the Alkhumra variant on the Arabian peninsula.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus murrayense
established.headline: Australian member of the Japanese encephalitis serocomplex.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus neudoerflense
established.headline: Principal cause of tick-borne encephalitis in Europe; vaccine-preventable.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus nilense
established.headline: Globally the most widespread encephalitic flavivirus, maintained in a bird–mosquito cycle.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus zikaense
established.headline: Flavivirus whose 2015–2016 American epidemic established it as a human teratogen.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus ilheusense
established.headline: Ilhéus and Rocio viruses. Rocio virus was isolated in 1975 from the cerebellum of a man who died of encephalitis, during an epidemic of roughly 1,000 cases across twenty coastal counties of São Paulo; Ilhéus virus has its own confirmed encephalitis cases.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus louisense
established.headline: St. Louis encephalitis virus. Encephalitis outbreaks in the Americas.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus omskense
established.headline: Omsk haemorrhagic fever virus. Tick- and muskrat-associated haemorrhagic fever.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus powassanense
established.headline: Powassan virus and deer tick virus. Severe tick-borne encephalitis in North America.

established.name: Orthoflavivirus zilberi
established.headline: Tick-borne encephalitis virus, Far Eastern and Siberian subtypes. Severe meningoencephalitis; vaccine-preventable.

established.name: Orthohantavirus andesense
established.headline: The only hantavirus with firmly documented person-to-person transmission.

established.name: Orthohantavirus hantanense
established.headline: Prototype hantavirus and cause of the severe form of haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in East Asia.

established.name: Orthohantavirus puumalaense
established.headline: Cause of nephropathia epidemica, the mild form of HFRS and the most common hantavirus disease in Europe.

established.name: Orthohantavirus sinnombreense
established.headline: Cause of hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in North America, identified during the 1993 Four Corners outbreak.

established.name: Orthohantavirus bayoui
established.headline: Bayou virus. HCPS with prominent renal involvement in the southern USA.

established.name: Orthohantavirus chocloense
established.headline: Choclo virus. HCPS and mild febrile illness in Panama.

established.name: Orthohantavirus dobravaense
established.headline: Dobrava-Belgrade virus. HFRS in the Balkans and central Europe.

established.name: Orthohantavirus mamorense
established.headline: Laguna Negra virus. HCPS in Paraguay and Bolivia.

established.name: Orthohantavirus nigrorivense
established.headline: Black Creek Canal virus. HCPS in Florida.

established.name: Orthohantavirus seoulense
established.headline: Seoul virus. HFRS worldwide, including rat-breeder outbreaks.

established.name: Orthohepacivirus hominis
established.headline: Roughly 50 million chronic infections, and the only chronic viral infection of humans that a short course of oral tablets reliably cures.

established.name: Orthohepadnavirus hominoidei
established.headline: 254 million people live with chronic hepatitis B, and it is a vaccine-preventable cause of cirrhosis and liver cancer that treatment controls but does not cure.

established.name: Paslahepevirus balayani
established.headline: The commonest cause of acute viral hepatitis worldwide, and two diseases in one species: a waterborne epidemic hepatitis of low-income settings, and a zoonotic foodborne infection of high-income ones.

established.name: Rocahepevirus ratti
established.headline: Rat hepatitis E virus (HEV-C1). Confirmed human hepatitis, first recognised in Hong Kong in 2018, mainly in immunocompromised and transplant patients; not detected by all HEV assays.

established.name: Deltavirus italiense
established.headline: A satellite virus that cannot replicate without hepatitis B surface antigen, and the most aggressive form of chronic viral hepatitis there is.

established.name: Deltavirus cameroonense
established.headline: Hepatitis D virus genotype 7. Central Africa.

established.name: Deltavirus carense
established.headline: Hepatitis D virus genotype 6. West and Central Africa.

established.name: Deltavirus japanense
established.headline: Hepatitis D virus genotype 2. East Asia; generally milder course than genotype 1.

established.name: Deltavirus peruense
established.headline: Hepatitis D virus genotype 3. Amazon basin; associated with fulminant hepatitis in outbreaks.

established.name: Deltavirus senegalense
established.headline: Hepatitis D virus genotype 8. West Africa and, through migration, South America.

established.name: Deltavirus taiwanense
established.headline: Hepatitis D virus genotype 4. Taiwan and Japan.

established.name: Deltavirus togense
established.headline: Hepatitis D virus genotype 5. West Africa; better interferon response reported.

established.name: Rubivirus rubellae
established.headline: Rubella virus. Rubella and congenital rubella syndrome; vaccine-preventable.

established.name: Orthonairovirus haemorrhagiae
established.headline: The most geographically widespread tick-borne virus causing human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen requiring high-level containment.

established.name: Cytomegalovirus humanbeta5
established.headline: Human cytomegalovirus. Congenital infection, and severe disease in transplant and HIV patients.

established.name: Lymphocryptovirus humangamma4
established.headline: Epstein-Barr virus. Infectious mononucleosis; Burkitt and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

established.name: Rhadinovirus humangamma8
established.headline: Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus. Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease.

established.name: Roseolovirus humanbeta6a
established.headline: Human herpesvirus 6A. Human infection established; disease associations less clear than 6B.

established.name: Roseolovirus humanbeta6b
established.headline: Human herpesvirus 6B. Roseola infantum and febrile seizures.

established.name: Roseolovirus humanbeta7
established.headline: Human herpesvirus 7. Roseola-like illness and febrile seizures in infancy.

established.name: Simplexvirus humanalpha1
established.headline: Herpes simplex virus 1. Orolabial and genital herpes, keratitis, encephalitis.

established.name: Simplexvirus humanalpha2
established.headline: Herpes simplex virus 2. Genital herpes and neonatal herpes.

established.name: Simplexvirus macacinealpha1
established.headline: Macacine alphaherpesvirus 1 (B virus). Rare but frequently fatal encephalomyelitis after macaque exposure.

established.name: Varicellovirus humanalpha3
established.headline: Varicella-zoster virus. Chickenpox and, on reactivation, shingles.

established.name: Alphainfluenzavirus influenzae
established.headline: Segmented orthomyxovirus with an avian reservoir, causing seasonal epidemics and periodic pandemics through antigenic shift and reassortment.

established.name: Betainfluenzavirus influenzae
established.headline: Influenza B virus. Seasonal influenza, disproportionately in children.

established.name: Gammainfluenzavirus influenzae
established.headline: Influenza C virus. Mild upper respiratory illness, mainly paediatric.

established.name: Thogotovirus bourbonense
established.headline: Bourbon virus. Tick-borne febrile illness with thrombocytopenia; fatal cases reported.

established.name: Alphapapillomavirus 10
established.headline: Includes HPV-6 and -11. Anogenital warts and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.

established.name: Alphapapillomavirus 7
established.headline: Includes HPV-18. Cervical adenocarcinoma and other anogenital cancers.

established.name: Alphapapillomavirus 9
established.headline: Includes HPV-16. Cervical, anogenital and oropharyngeal carcinoma; vaccine-preventable.

established.name: Mupapillomavirus 1
established.headline: HPV-1. Plantar and common warts.

established.name: Henipavirus hendraense
established.headline: Australian henipavirus transmitted from flying foxes via horses; rare but highly lethal in humans.

established.name: Henipavirus nipahense
established.headline: Bat-borne paramyxovirus with case fatality of 40–75% and documented person-to-person transmission; a WHO priority pathogen requiring BSL-4 handling.

established.name: Morbillivirus hominis
established.headline: One of the most contagious human viruses (R0 of 12–18), vaccine-preventable, and a cause of lasting immune amnesia.

established.name: Orthorubulavirus hominis
established.headline: Human parainfluenza virus 4A/4B. Mild to moderate respiratory illness.

established.name: Orthorubulavirus laryngotracheitidis
established.headline: Human parainfluenza virus 2. Croup and upper respiratory illness in children.

established.name: Orthorubulavirus parotitidis
established.headline: Mumps virus. Parotitis, orchitis, meningitis; vaccine-preventable.

established.name: Respirovirus laryngotracheitidis
established.headline: Human parainfluenza virus 1. Leading cause of croup.

established.name: Respirovirus pneumoniae
established.headline: Human parainfluenza virus 3. Bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants.

established.name: Erythroparvovirus primate1
established.headline: Parvovirus B19. Fifth disease, transient aplastic crisis, hydrops fetalis.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus bunyamweraense
established.headline: Prototype orthobunyavirus. Its reassortant member Ngari virus (Bunyamwera backbone with Batai M segment) causes haemorrhagic fever in East Africa.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus bwambaense
established.headline: Highly prevalent African orthobunyavirus causing undifferentiated fever; seroprevalence exceeds 50% in parts of East Africa.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus cacheense
established.headline: North American Bunyamwera-serogroup virus; a teratogen in sheep and a rare cause of severe human neuroinvasive disease.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus caraparuense
established.headline: Group C orthobunyavirus; a frequent cause of acute febrile illness among forest workers in the Amazon.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus encephalitidis
established.headline: Prototype of the California serogroup; historically important, now a rare cause of human encephalitis compared with La Crosse virus.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus guaroaense
established.headline: Natural reassortant bridging the California and Bunyamwera serogroups; a recognised cause of febrile illness in South America.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus ileshaense
established.headline: Bunyamwera-serogroup virus isolated from African febrile patients, with rare reports of haemorrhagic and neurological presentations.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus jamestownense
established.headline: California-serogroup virus causing febrile and neuroinvasive disease mainly in adults in North America; Inkoo virus is its Eurasian counterpart.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus lacrosseense
established.headline: Leading cause of paediatric arboviral encephalitis in the United States, in the California serogroup.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus oribocaense
established.headline: Group C viruses repeatedly isolated from febrile Amazonian patients.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense
established.headline: The most important human pathogen of the Simbu serogroup and, after dengue, one of the most frequent arboviral febrile illnesses in the Amazon basin. Major expansion across the Americas from 2023–2024.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus tahynaense
established.headline: European California-serogroup virus causing 'Valtice fever'.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus apeuense
established.headline: Apeú virus. Febrile illness in Brazil.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus madridense
established.headline: Madrid virus. Febrile illness in Panama.

established.name: Orthobunyavirus maritubaense
established.headline: Marituba virus. Febrile illness in Amazonia.

established.name: Bandavirus dabieense
established.common: severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV)
established.headline: Tick-borne bandavirus causing a severe haemorrhagic febrile illness in East Asia, with case fatality of roughly 5–30%.

established.name: Bandavirus heartlandense
established.headline: North American counterpart of SFTSV, transmitted by the lone star tick.

established.name: Phlebovirus riftense
established.headline: Zoonotic phlebovirus causing devastating ruminant abortion storms and human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen.

established.name: Phlebovirus toscanaense
established.headline: A leading cause of summer aseptic meningitis around the Mediterranean, transmitted by sandflies.

established.name: Phlebovirus napoliense
established.headline: Sandfly fever Naples virus. Three-day fever.

established.name: Phlebovirus siciliaense
established.headline: Sandfly fever Sicilian virus. Three-day fever.

established.name: Phlebovirus toroense
established.headline: Punta Toro virus. Febrile illness in Panama and Colombia.

established.name: Hepatovirus ahepa
established.headline: A faecal-oral hepatitis that never becomes chronic, is entirely vaccine-preventable, and gets more dangerous the later in life it is acquired.

established.name: Enterovirus alphacoxsackie
established.headline: Coxsackievirus A serotypes. Hand-foot-and-mouth disease, herpangina, aseptic meningitis.

established.name: Enterovirus alpharhino
established.headline: Rhinovirus A. Common cold; asthma and COPD exacerbation.

established.name: Enterovirus betacoxsackie
established.headline: Coxsackievirus B and echoviruses. Myocarditis, pleurodynia, aseptic meningitis, neonatal sepsis.

established.name: Enterovirus betarhino
established.headline: Rhinovirus B. Common cold, generally milder than A or C.

established.name: Enterovirus cerhino
established.headline: Rhinovirus C. Common cold with a higher rate of lower respiratory involvement in children.

established.name: Enterovirus coxsackiepol
established.headline: Includes poliovirus 1-3 and coxsackie A serotypes: poliomyelitis, herpangina, hand-foot-and-mouth disease.

established.name: Enterovirus deconjuncti
established.headline: Enterovirus D68 and D70. Severe respiratory illness with acute flaccid myelitis; epidemic conjunctivitis.

established.name: Kobuvirus aichi
established.headline: Aichivirus A. Oyster-associated and travel-associated gastroenteritis.

established.name: Parechovirus ahumpari
established.headline: Human parechovirus 1-6. Gastroenteritis and, as HPeV-3, neonatal sepsis and meningoencephalitis.

established.name: Orthopneumovirus hominis
established.headline: The leading cause of infant bronchiolitis worldwide and a major cause of severe respiratory disease in older adults — and, after sixty years of failure, now preventable at both ends of life.

established.name: Metapneumovirus hominis
established.headline: Human metapneumovirus. Bronchiolitis and pneumonia across all ages.

established.name: Alphapolyomavirus quintihominis
established.headline: Merkel cell polyomavirus. Clonally integrated in most Merkel cell carcinomas.

established.name: Betapolyomavirus hominis
established.headline: BK polyomavirus. Polyomavirus-associated nephropathy and haemorrhagic cystitis after transplantation.

established.name: Betapolyomavirus secuhominis
established.headline: JC polyomavirus. Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in immunosuppression.

established.name: Orthopoxvirus monkeypox
established.headline: Orthopoxvirus causing mpox; clade I is more virulent, clade II drove the 2022 global outbreak through sexual networks.

established.name: Orthopoxvirus variola
established.headline: Cause of smallpox — the only human disease ever eradicated (certified 1980). Retained only in two WHO-authorised repositories.

established.name: Molluscipoxvirus molluscum
established.headline: Molluscum contagiosum virus. Umbilicated papules, common in children and in HIV.

established.name: Orthopoxvirus cowpox
established.headline: Cowpox virus. Localised ulcerating lesions, usually from cats; severe in the immunocompromised.

established.name: Orthopoxvirus vaccinia
established.headline: Vaccinia virus. Vaccine strain; causes progressive vaccinia, eczema vaccinatum and buffalopox.

established.name: Parapoxvirus bovinestomatitis
established.headline: Bovine papular stomatitis virus. Occupational hand lesions.

established.name: Parapoxvirus orf
established.headline: Orf virus. Contagious pustular dermatitis; occupational hand lesions in sheep handlers.

established.name: Parapoxvirus pseudocowpox
established.headline: Pseudocowpox virus. Milker's nodule.

established.name: Parapoxvirus sealpox
established.headline: Sealpox virus. Occupational nodular skin lesions in seal handlers.

established.name: Yatapoxvirus tanapox
established.headline: Tanapox and Yaba-like disease viruses. Febrile illness with a nodular skin lesion.

established.name: Deltaretrovirus priTlym1
established.headline: The first human retrovirus discovered, infecting 5-10 million people. Most carry it for life without consequence; a minority develop adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma after decades, or a progressive myelopathy.

established.name: Lentivirus humimdef1
established.headline: Retrovirus causing AIDS; roughly 40 million people live with HIV and antiretroviral therapy has transformed it into a manageable chronic infection.

established.name: Lentivirus humimdef2
established.headline: A West African lentivirus from sooty mangabeys, less transmissible and slower to progress than HIV-1, and intrinsically resistant to two whole antiretroviral classes.

established.name: Lyssavirus rabies
established.headline: Effectively 100% fatal once clinical, yet entirely preventable by prompt post-exposure prophylaxis; ~59,000 deaths annually, mostly from dog bites.

established.name: Lyssavirus australis
established.headline: Australian bat lyssavirus. Rabies-like fatal encephalitis.

established.name: Lyssavirus duvenhage
established.headline: Duvenhage virus. Fatal rabies-like encephalitis after bat contact.

established.name: Lyssavirus hamburg
established.headline: European bat lyssavirus 1. Fatal rabies-like encephalitis.

established.name: Lyssavirus helsinki
established.headline: European bat lyssavirus 2. Fatal rabies-like encephalitis in bat handlers.

established.name: Lyssavirus irkut
established.headline: Irkut virus. Fatal human encephalitis reported in Russia and China.

established.name: Lyssavirus mokola
established.headline: Mokola virus. Rabies-like fatal encephalitis; human cases reported in Nigeria and Zimbabwe. Critically, it is not neutralised by rabies vaccine-induced antibody, so standard post-exposure prophylaxis cannot be relied on.

established.name: Vesiculovirus chandipura
established.headline: Chandipura virus. Outbreaks of acute encephalitis with high mortality in Indian children.

established.name: Vesiculovirus indiana
established.headline: Vesicular stomatitis Indiana virus. Influenza-like illness in exposed livestock and laboratory workers.

established.name: Vesiculovirus newjersey
established.headline: Vesicular stomatitis New Jersey virus. Influenza-like occupational illness.

established.name: Rotavirus alphagastroenteritidis
established.headline: Rotavirus A. Leading cause of severe childhood diarrhoea; vaccine-preventable.

established.name: Rotavirus betagastroenteritidis
established.headline: Rotavirus B. Adult diarrhoea outbreaks, described chiefly in China.

established.name: Rotavirus tritogastroenteritidis
established.headline: Rotavirus C. Sporadic cases and family or school outbreaks of gastroenteritis.

established.name: Coltivirus dermacentoris
established.headline: Colorado tick fever virus. The commonest tick-borne viral infection of the western United States: biphasic 'saddleback' fever with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, the virus persisting in erythrocytes for weeks after recovery, which is why blood donation is deferred.

established.name: Alphavirus chikungunya
established.headline: Alphavirus of the Semliki Forest complex causing explosive epidemics of febrile polyarthritis.

established.name: Alphavirus eastern
established.serogroup: New World: eastern equine encephalitis complex
established.headline: The most lethal arbovirus endemic to North America.

established.name: Alphavirus rossriver
established.headline: The most commonly notified arboviral infection in Australia.

established.name: Alphavirus venezuelan
established.common: Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV), subtypes IAB/IC/ID/IE
established.serogroup: New World: Venezuelan equine encephalitis complex
established.headline: Epizootic alphavirus causing large human and equine outbreaks in the Americas; also a classical laboratory-acquired infection.

established.name: Alphavirus barmah
established.headline: Barmah Forest virus. Fever, rash and polyarthritis in Australia.

established.name: Alphavirus mayaro
established.headline: Mayaro virus. Febrile arthralgic illness in South America.

established.name: Alphavirus onyong
established.headline: O'nyong-nyong virus. Large epidemics of fever, rash and arthralgia in Africa.

established.name: Alphavirus sindbis
established.serogroup: New World: western equine encephalitis complex
established.headline: Sindbis virus. Pogosta/Ockelbo disease: fever, rash and arthralgia.

established.name: Alphavirus western
established.serogroup: New World: western equine encephalitis complex
established.headline: Western equine encephalitis virus. Encephalitis in the Americas.

probable.name: Mamastrovirus homustovis
probable.headline: Human astrovirus MLB/VA clades. Detected in gastroenteritis and in encephalitis cases in the immunocompromised.

probable.name: Orthoflavivirus usutuense
probable.headline: Usutu virus. Human neuroinvasive cases and blood-donor seropositivity in Europe.

probable.name: Orthonairovirus kasokeroense
probable.headline: Kasokero virus. Laboratory and bat-exposure febrile illness in Uganda.

probable.name: Orthonairovirus songlingense
probable.headline: Songling virus. Febrile illness with headache reported in north-eastern China.

probable.name: Orthonairovirus tachengense
probable.headline: Tacheng tick virus 1. Human febrile cases reported in Xinjiang.

probable.name: Bocaparvovirus primate1
probable.headline: Human bocavirus 1. Frequently found in paediatric respiratory illness; causation debated given high co-detection.

probable.name: Orthobunyavirus bataiense
probable.headline: Widespread Bunyamwera-serogroup virus of Eurasia and Africa; donor of the M segment that created Ngari virus.

probable.name: Orthobunyavirus catqueense
probable.headline: Simbu-serogroup orthobunyavirus of the Manzanilla clade, maintained in pigs and Culicoides biting midges across East and South Asia. Known mainly from swine serosurveys and vector surveillance; a single 2026 report describes severe human disease.

probable.name: Orthobunyavirus khatangaense
probable.headline: California-serogroup virus of boreal North America and Eurasia.

probable.name: Orthobunyavirus tataguineense
probable.headline: African orthobunyavirus recovered from febrile patients with rash.

probable.name: Cardiovirus saffoldi
probable.headline: Saffold virus. Repeatedly recovered from children with respiratory and enteric illness; causation not settled.

probable.name: Salivirus aklasse
probable.headline: Salivirus A. Detected in children with acute diarrhoea; association reported but not established.

probable.name: Alphapolyomavirus octihominis
probable.headline: Trichodysplasia spinulosa polyomavirus. Associated with trichodysplasia spinulosa in immunosuppressed patients.

probable.name: Orthopoxvirus akhmetapox
probable.headline: Akhmeta virus. Human skin lesions reported in Georgia.

probable.name: Deltaretrovirus priTlym2
probable.headline: HTLV-2. Infection is established and routinely confirmed by PCR, endemic in Amerindian and injecting-drug-using populations; a myelopathy resembling HAM/TSP is reported, but the association is weaker than for HTLV-1 and there is no leukaemia link.

probable.name: Ledantevirus kern
probable.headline: Kern Canyon-related; Oita/Fikirini group bat rhabdoviruses with sparse human data.

probable.name: Lyssavirus caucasicus
probable.headline: West Caucasian bat virus. No human case; vaccine escape makes exposure consequential.

probable.name: Orbivirus orungoense
probable.headline: Orungo virus. Febrile illness in West Africa.

probable.name: Seadornavirus bannaense
probable.headline: Banna virus. Isolated from patients with encephalitis and fever in China.

probable.name: Alphavirus everglades
probable.serogroup: New World: Venezuelan equine encephalitis complex
probable.headline: Everglades virus. VEE complex; human febrile illness in Florida.

probable.name: Alphavirus madariaga
probable.serogroup: New World: eastern equine encephalitis complex
probable.headline: Madariaga virus. South American EEE lineage; human encephalitis reported in Panama.

probable.name: Alphavirus mucambo
probable.serogroup: New World: Venezuelan equine encephalitis complex
probable.headline: Mucambo virus. VEE complex; sporadic human febrile illness.

probable.name: Alphavirus tonate
probable.serogroup: New World: Venezuelan equine encephalitis complex
probable.headline: Tonate virus. VEE complex; human encephalitis reported in French Guiana.

possible.name: Mastadenovirus adami

animal-only.name: Orthoebolavirus restonense
animal-only.headline: Reston virus. Lethal in macaques and infects pigs; documented asymptomatic seroconversion in exposed human handlers but no human disease in over 30 years. Animal pathogen with proven human exposure, which is not the same as no human infection.

animal-only.name: Orthoflavivirus tembusu
animal-only.headline: Tembusu virus. Duck pathogen of major veterinary importance; human infection unproven.

animal-only.name: Orthobunyavirus akabaneense
animal-only.headline: Classical teratogenic Simbu-serogroup virus of ruminants; the cause of epizootic arthrogryposis–hydranencephaly in cattle, sheep and goats.

animal-only.name: Orthobunyavirus schmallenbergense
animal-only.headline: Emerged in northwest Europe in 2011 as a ruminant teratogen; extensive human serosurveys of exposed farmers and veterinarians have found no convincing evidence of human infection.

animal-only.name: Orthopoxvirus ectromelia
animal-only.headline: Ectromelia virus. Mousepox; a major laboratory-animal pathogen.

animal-only.name: Orbivirus ruminantium
animal-only.headline: Bluetongue virus. Major ruminant pathogen; no human disease.

animal-only.name: Alphavirus getah
animal-only.headline: Getah virus. Disease in horses and pigs; human seropositivity without confirmed illness.

established.label: Established human pathogen
established.note: Virus isolated or amplified from symptomatic humans with an accepted causal link to a defined syndrome.

probable.label: Probable human pathogen
probable.note: Human infection confirmed by isolation, RT-PCR or seroconversion alongside compatible illness; causation not fully settled.

possible.label: Possible / under investigation
possible.note: Serological evidence of human exposure, or isolated case reports; clinical significance unresolved.

animal-only.label: Animal pathogen, no human disease
animal-only.note: Veterinary importance with no credible evidence of human disease despite exposure.

no-evidence.label: No human evidence
no-evidence.note: No reported human infection. For almost all of the species here that is because the host range does not include vertebrates at all, and `basis` says so; for a handful it is a vertebrate virus nobody has been infected by. Either way this is a claim about the evidence, not an absence of one.

unassessed.label: Not assessed
unassessed.note: No assessment has been made here. Absence of a profile is not evidence against human infection.
